entry.title: Can we read Huginn’s latent thoughts? It depends on the lens

link.title: Can we read Huginn’s latent thoughts? It depends on the lens

entry.content:
This week’s paper claims that looping a recurrent block is a form of reasoning in latent space. If that is true, we should be able to watch the answer form across the recurrences. Two papers tried to do this on Huginn, the model from this week’s paper.

Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer (Lu, Yang, Lee, Li & Liu, 2025): Decodes Huginn’s intermediate states with the logit lens and with a coda lens, which runs the state through Huginn’s own two learned decoder blocks. The two lenses disagree about which recurrent blocks are readable, and neither shows a clear latent chain of thought.

Looped Transformers under the Jacobian Lens: Does the Global Workspace Survive Recurrence? (anonymous ICLR 2027 submission, under review): Fits a lens aimed at each stage of the loop and finds the answer is readable at every recurrence. Each lens can only read about two recurrences ahead, though, so a lens that fails on early states says nothing about whether those states contain the answer. (Caveat - still under review. This looks good and highly relevant, but we should probably wait for a peer-reviewed version)

Why the two papers seem to disagree

The Jacobian lens is a linear map: the average, over many prompts, of how a change in one hidden state moves a later one. A logit-lens or coda-lens readout asks the early state to look like the final one. The Jacobian lens instead learns how to carry the early state forward to a chosen target recurrence (4, 8, 12 or 16) and reads it there.

On “The capital city of the country famous for sushi is”, Tokyo ranks first at recurrences 2–3 through the lens aimed at recurrence 4. Through the lenses aimed at 8, 12 and 16 it ranks first at recurrences 7, 10–11 and 14–15. The same forward pass looks empty or full depending on which lens you use and how far it has to reach. That is one explanation for the disagreement Lu et al. saw.

Here a recurrence is one pass of Huginn’s 4-layer core, so “two recurrences” is about 8 transformer layers.

What the model seems to be doing

  • It recomputes rather than remembers. Shrinking the input that Huginn re-injects at every recurrence to a quarter of its size breaks the answer on every tested prompt. Swapping in another prompt’s input changes the answer within about two recurrences.
  • It can steer old content but can’t report new content. If you swap a concept the model already computed, it reports the new one 98% of the time (124/126). If you inject a concept it never computed, it never names it (0/97). Ouro, a looped model trained to be readable after every loop, manages 31%.
  • Only late edits stick. Edits in the last lens window are as effective as edits everywhere (25/192 flips each). Edits in the window before it get 5/192.

Questions for class

  • If the answer is readable from recurrence 2–3, what are the remaining recurrences doing? Is that “reasoning”, or re-deriving the same answer from the input?
  • The paper’s convergent, orbiting and drifting trajectories (Figure 12): does “the state keeps being rebuilt from the input” change how we read them?
  • How much of what we call latent reasoning is a property of the model, and how much of the instrument we use to look?

Bonus, if you care about compute: What Does Another Loop Buy? (anonymous ICLR 2027 submission) stops looping once the attention pattern stops changing between iterations. On Huginn it saves 48% of the compute for a 2-point drop on GSM8K, and beats a KL-based exit at matched compute. That is a simple alternative to the early-exit criterion in this week’s paper.
entry.summary: Two papers that try to decode the recurrent states of this week's model, and why they seem to disagree.

entry.title: A better graph instead of Table 4

link.title: A better graph instead of Table 4

entry.content:
The original

Table 4 in Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach (Geiping et al., 2025) compares recurrent models with a fixed-depth Transformer baseline across several benchmarks.

The table is useful for looking up exact scores, but it makes the reader work to see the improvement over the baseline. For each benchmark, we must find the relevant rows, subtract their scores, and remember the difference while moving to the next column.

The redesign

The redesigned chart focuses on “Ours early ckpt” at r=1 and r=32, compared with the fixed-depth baseline. All three rows use 180B training tokens; the later 800B-token checkpoints are excluded.

Each bar shows recurrent accuracy minus baseline accuracy, in percentage points, rather than a relative percentage improvement. For example, HellaSwag changes from 37.34% for the baseline to 29.19% at r=1 and 48.80% at r=32: the bars therefore show −8.15 and +11.46 percentage points.

The chart preserves the table’s benchmark order and includes all ten metrics. The two GSM8K columns are labeled separately as GSM8K CoT (Strict) and GSM8K CoT (Flexible).

What changed and why

  • A shared zero line makes the comparison immediate. Bars extending right indicate improvement over the baseline; bars extending left indicate lower accuracy.
  • Paired blue and orange bars reveal the effect of depth. Each benchmark places r=1 beside r=32, so the reader can compare their direction and magnitude without scanning between table rows.
  • Matching training-token counts keeps the scope clear. Equal training tokens do not imply equal training FLOPs, so this is a comparison at a matched token budget.

The result is easier to process because the reader can see the differences instead of calculating them mentally. The overall pattern is visible at a glance: r=32 beats the fixed-depth baseline on every displayed metric, whereas r=1 falls below it on nine of ten. The exception is also visible: WinoGrande improves by +1.97 points at r=1 and +1.10 at r=32, so increasing depth does not improve every benchmark. The chart reduces the arithmetic and memory needed to understand both the main pattern and its exception.
entry.summary: Turning Table 4 into a diverging bar chart makes the effect of recurrent depth easier to compare across benchmarks.

entry.title: Connecting trajectories and predictions
entry.content:
The original

Figure 12 shows what the model does internally as it uses more computation. The figure shows selected tokens moving through latent space over recurrent steps. Some trajectories appear to converge, whereas others orbit or drift. How do these movements relate to changes in the model’s predictions?

The original shows three pairs of principal components: PC1–PC2, PC3–PC4, and PC5–PC6. These are only three of the fifteen possible pairs among the first six components. A loop can look narrow or nearly line-like in one projection and open up in another, so how we choose the planes affects how we perceive the geometry.

The input passages are also difficult to find, e.g., the arithmetic question appears in the caption of Figure 16, but not in Figure 12. Finally, the trajectories alone do not seem to be showing if the model’s prediction changes during the recurrence process.

The redesign

Note that this is a design demonstration using synthetic trajectories and probabilities, since I did not find the activations in their repository. The additional projections and probability crossings shown here are therefore visual examples, not recovered measurements or new findings about the model.

I replace each set of three projections with a corner plot showing all fifteen pairs. A probability inset and a star marker show when we move from the initial to the final prediction of the model.

Figure 12. Orbital and convergent trajectories across recurrent steps. Each recurrent step reapplies the same transformer block to update hidden states while the input sequence remains fixed. Here, $r$ counts internal iterations. The corner plot shows the orbital dynamics from token “3” in “Claire makes a 3 egg omelet every morning for breakfast. How many dozens of eggs will she eat in 4 weeks?”. We show all 15 pairwise views of the six principal-component (PC) coordinates. Color denotes $r=0$–128. Open circles and filled squares mark initial and final states. Insets track synthetic probabilities of two fixed candidate tokens at a fixed readout positions. Stars mark their first overtake in both the inset and trajectory ($r_\star=54$ in A and $18$ in B).

What changed and why

  • Showing the fifteen component pairs makes the dependence on projection easier to inspect.
  • A recurrence colorbar and endpoint markers make the progression of the trajectory more clear.
  • A probability inset with a star marker connects the change in response event to its location along the trajectory.
  • The caption shows the exact sentence used in the experiment and briefly explains what we are tracking, without having to read all the paper to understand it.
entry.summary: Showing all component pairs and linking recurrent steps to prediction probabilities.

entry.title: LearningHarness: Optimize your learning with AI

link.title: LearningHarness: Optimize your learning with AI

entry.content:
I’ve decided to focus my learning post this week on a tool I’ve recently been exposed to called Learning Harness. This tool, which plugs into your preferred LLM, promises to streamline learning using AI, allowing you to focus your time on the critical learning stage, where you can gain the most. The tool breaks down the learning objective into smaller, manageable steps, avoiding the usual “wall of text” encountered when trying to learn something new with LLMs.

Here I’ll share my experience learning this week’s paper and its surrounding context using LearningHarness:

The learning process begins with your request. I asked: “I want to be prepared and brought up to speed to read this paper. I want to know anything that the standard reader this paper is intended for should know before diving in and then I want you to walk me through the paper completely so that I know all the important details (not looking to reimplement this or anything, but I want to understand the mechanisms ideas and any math such that I could intelligently participate in a discussion on the paper)”.

Next comes the probing stage. To identify your current knowledge and personalize an efficient learning plan, the model tests your knowledge in different areas related to the requested lesson. The harness allows you to record your thoughts and confidance while going through these questions, helping it identify the edges of your knowledge. The questions adapt to your previous answers and recorded thinking. This process took about an hour for me and included 20 questions, and should take less once previous learning sessions have already built a good understanding of your preexisting knowledge.

Once mapping what you already know has been completed, the harness designs a tree of ideas/logical-steps towards your learning goal and the dependency relations between them:

Learning begins. The model will walk you through one idea at a time. Providing short explanations followed by a question meant to check your understanding or build intuition towards the next point. Example learning step:

What I liked

  1. The harness pulls additional resources from various online sources/papers so that it doesn’t only walk you through the paper but also through the motivation.
  2. Being able to record your thinking and answers allows much better communication of the gaps in your understanding. Sometimes answering a question might be easy from context but you can point out that some details of the question and or definitions around it are unclear.
  3. The small learning steps are great, they truly are almost atomic pieces of knowledge. This makes learning more fun than just reading a long page of text, and provides much more friction points to test understanding.
  4. where gaps in the paper exist, like failed runs that aren’t addressed or explained. The model tries to provide intuition, clearly admitting it doesn’t exist in the paper.

What I didn’t like

  1. Bugs: sometimes the agent fails to output the correct format, resulting in some learning text missing or tables/graphs not being properly rendered.
  2. Not enough visualizations. seems like there’s supposed to be an animator agent functionality but I didn’t really get to see it in action much.
  3. The paper is rarely directly cited, making it at times unclear what information is grounded in the paper and what isn’t.

##TLDR LearningHarness is a cool tool showing a lot of potential in optimizing learning in the AI era. While still unpolished, it offers great value in making a more unique and interactive learning experience than online research. It seems to me this tool would be most suited for learning topics that aren’t grounded in a single paper, but are spread across many sources and can be combined into a single line of knowledge. I will keep using LearningHarness and I reccoment you try it too

Learn more

link to youtube video

link to github repo to download

Shout-out to David Plotkin for introducing me to this tool.
entry.summary: My experience using an AI learning tool to read this paper.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
Papers worth knowing

  1. Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT (2026): Introduces a 4-billion-parameter recurrent language model that uses elastic depth, difficulty-aware loop allocation, and reinforcement learning to improve reasoning performance while reducing generated tokens.

  2. Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models (2026): Introduces LARC, a framework that enables multimodal models to perform reasoning directly in continuous latent space, improving image generation quality and enabling test-time compute scaling.

  3. Learning When to Think Aloud in Latent Reasoning (2026): Introduces VITAL, a hybrid reasoning framework that selectively generates important intermediate tokens while performing the remaining reasoning in latent space, improving the balance between reasoning accuracy and token efficiency.
entry.summary: Recent work extends recurrent latent reasoning to large-scale language models, multimodal generation, and hybrid reasoning.

entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning

link.title: Rewriting the abstract of Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract is short and clear, but it is mostly claims without evidence. It says the model improves “sometimes dramatically” and that it can capture reasoning “not easily represented in words”, yet it gives no number, no benchmark, and no comparison. A reader cannot tell what “dramatically” means, or on which tasks it happens. It also defines the method only through what it is not (it is not chain-of-thought), and it states the compute as “equivalent to 50 billion parameters” without saying that the model itself has only 3.5 billion.

The rewrite (1) opens with the one-sentence idea, thinking by looping instead of by writing more tokens, (2) explains what “latent reasoning” means in plain words, (3) replaces “sometimes dramatically” with the paper’s own comparison against an identical non-recurrent model, and (4) says where the gains are large and where they are not.

Before and after

Before: We study a novel language model architecture that is capable of scaling test-time computation by implicitly reasoning in latent space. Our model works by iterating a recurrent block, thereby unrolling to arbitrary depth at test-time. This stands in contrast to mainstream reasoning models that scale up compute by producing more tokens. Unlike approaches based on chain-of-thought, our approach does not require any specialized training data, can work with small context windows, and can capture types of reasoning that are not easily represented in words. We scale a proof-of-concept model to 3.5 billion parameters and 800 billion tokens. We show that the resulting model can improve its performance on reasoning benchmarks, sometimes dramatically, up to a computation load equivalent to 50 billion parameters.
After: Today's reasoning models think by writing more tokens. We show a language model can think by looping instead: a block of layers is repeated as many times as needed at test time, so the model reasons in its hidden state and produces no extra text. This needs no chain-of-thought training data, works with a small context window, and is not limited to reasoning that can be put into words. We train a 3.5B-parameter proof of concept on 800B tokens. Giving it more iterations raises its accuracy on reasoning benchmarks, up to a compute budget equal to a 50B-parameter model. The gains are largest on hard tasks: on GSM8K, an early checkpoint of the recurrent model is already 5 times better than a non-recurrent model trained in exactly the same setting, while easy tasks such as HellaSwag stop improving after about 8 iterations.

A title to match. The current title, Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach, is accurate but long, and “latent reasoning” and “recurrent depth” are two names for one idea. A shorter alternative that gives the mechanism and the benefit: Thinking in Loops: Scaling Test-Time Compute by Iterating Layers, Not Tokens.

The general rule

  1. Replace vague strength with a comparison. “Sometimes dramatically” asks the reader to trust you; “5 times better than the same model without recurrence” lets them check.
  2. Say what the method is, not only what it is not. The original defines the model by contrast with chain-of-thought. The rewrite first says what it does (repeats a block of layers), and uses the contrast only to explain the benefit.
  3. Say where it works and where it does not. An honest limit (“easy tasks stop improving after about 8 iterations”) makes the strong result more believable.
  4. Give both numbers that a figure needs. “Compute equivalent to 50B parameters” means little unless the reader also knows the model has 3.5B.

What I’m unsure about

The rewrite drops the phrase “novel language model architecture”, and I do not claim the reasoning happens “without words” in a strong sense, since the paper does not show what the latent iterations contain. I also chose the GSM8K comparison because it is the paper’s clearest one, but it comes from an early 180B-token checkpoint and not from the final 800B-token model. Whether that is the fairest number to put in an abstract is worth arguing about in class.

Paper: arXiv:2502.05171.
entry.summary: The abstract promises dramatic gains but never shows one. Here is a version that says what the model does, what it costs, and where the gains actually appear.

entry.title: Literature Review: Recurrent Depth and Latent Reasoning

link.title: Literature Review: Recurrent Depth and Latent Reasoning

entry.content:
The papers this builds on

Recurrent computation offers a way to increase a network’s effective depth while reusing its parameters. Universal Transformers introduced repeated, shared self-attention transformations across depth (Dehghani et al., 2019). Subsequent work showed that recurrent networks trained on simple problems could solve harder instances by performing more iterations at inference time (Schwarzschild et al., 2021). However, additional iterations can also degrade performance. Bansal et al. (2022) addressed this “overthinking” problem through input recall and progressive training.

These ideas connect to algorithmic reasoning and in-context learning. Giannou et al. (2023) demonstrated theoretically how looped Transformers can execute iterative algorithms, while Yang et al. (2024) showed that trained looped Transformers can match standard Transformers on several in-context learning tasks using substantially fewer parameters.

Geiping et al. (2025) bring recurrent-depth modeling to a 3.5-billion-parameter language model trained on approximately 800 billion tokens. Their model repeatedly applies a shared Transformer block to hidden representations. Randomized training depths and stabilization techniques enable performance gains from additional inference-time iterations, especially on mathematics and coding tasks. Its central contribution is demonstrating this approach at substantial language-model scale, without requiring specialized reasoning supervision.

The fields and concepts it connects to

A related research direction moves reasoning away from explicit text: Deng et al. (2024) gradually internalize chain-of-thought (CoT) steps; Cheng and Van Durme (2024) compress reasoning into continuous representations; and Hao et al. (2025) feed hidden states back as subsequent input embeddings. Concurrently, Saunshi et al. (2025) provide theoretical and empirical evidence for looped Transformers’ reasoning capabilities.

Together, these connections position recurrent depth as a complementary route to test-time scaling alongside explicit CoT. My main takeaway is that Geiping et al. establish the feasibility of large-scale recurrent reasoning; establishing when it offers the best accuracy–compute trade-off remains a separate question.
entry.summary: How recurrent networks, looped Transformers, and implicit reasoning lead to test-time scaling in latent space.

entry.title: Reproducing Figure 3: How often is each recurrence depth sampled?

link.title: Reproducing Figure 3: How often is each recurrence depth sampled?

entry.content:
What I reimplemented

During training, the authors sample how many times to run the recurrent block. I reproduced Figure 3 by implementing the sampling rule from Section 3.3 and drawing one million recurrence counts with $\bar r = 32$ and $\sigma = 0.5$. Paper, Section 3.3

The code

Each draw starts with a normal random variable tau. Its exponential gives the rate for a Poisson draw. Adding one ensures that the recurrent block runs at least once.

mu = np.log(r_bar) - sigma**2 / 2
tau = rng.normal(loc=mu, scale=sigma, size=n)
rate = np.exp(tau)
r = rng.poisson(lam=rate) + 1

Full code and results (Jupyter notebook)

Results

Statistic Figure 3 Reproduction
Mean 33.0 33.002
Median 29 29
Mode 24 24

All three statistics match Figure 3 at the precision reported in the paper.

What I learned

The most common training depth was 24, even though the average was 33. The histogram shows why: occasional draws with many recurrences pull the mean above both the mode and the median. Seeing all three on the same plot made the training schedule easier to interpret.
entry.summary: Reproducing the distribution of training depths from Section 3.3.

entry.title: Can we make machine think more like humans

link.title: Can we make machine think more like humans

entry.content:
Motivation

When we solve a problem, we don’t always approach it in the same way. Some questions are simple enough that we can answer them almost immediately. Others require us to stop and think for a while.

What’s interesting is that we can often estimate how much effort a question will require before we even start solving it. But that estimate isn’t always right. Sometimes a problem looks easy at first, and only after working on it do we realize that we need to think more deeply.

There is another aspect of human reasoning that I find particularly interesting: when a problem becomes too complicated to solve entirely in our heads, we take out a pen and paper.

Writing down intermediate calculations allows us to break a difficult problem into smaller parts, keep track of what we have already discovered, and use those results later. We don’t necessarily write down every thought. We usually start writing when we feel that doing everything mentally is becoming difficult.

I think there is a natural connection between this behavior and reasoning in language models.

The Huginn paper introduces a recurrent Transformer that can perform additional computation in its hidden states before predicting the next token. This resembles the internal part of human reasoning: thinking without necessarily saying or writing anything.

On the other hand, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can be viewed as the model’s pen and paper. By generating intermediate reasoning steps, the model creates information that it can refer to when making subsequent predictions.

This raises a question:

Instead of forcing a language model to always think for a fixed amount of time or always generate Chain-of-Thought, can we teach it to decide when each approach is useful?

Proposed Idea: A Reasoning Controller

I propose extending Huginn with a single lightweight controller that dynamically decides how the model should allocate its reasoning computation.

The controller would operate both before and during the reasoning process.

Initially, it would examine the question’s representation, produced by Huginn’s prelude, and estimate how much internal computation is needed. Rather than committing to a fixed budget, it would choose an action and then reevaluate the situation after that action has been completed.

As Huginn continues reasoning, the same controller would examine its updated hidden state and decide what to do next.

The controller would have four possible actions:

  • THINK(4): Perform four additional recurrent iterations without generating text.
  • THINK(8): Perform eight additional recurrent iterations without generating text.
  • WRITE: Generate an intermediate reasoning step, similar to writing something down on paper.
  • ANSWER: Stop reasoning and generate the final answer.

We define the action space as:

\[\mathcal{A}= \{\operatorname{THINK}(4),\operatorname{THINK}(8), \operatorname{WRITE},\operatorname{ANSWER}\}.\]

At the beginning, the controller primarily uses the question’s representation to make an initial decision. After recurrent iterations have been performed, it can also use the information accumulated in Huginn’s hidden state.

For example, the model could choose:

\[\operatorname{THINK}(8) \rightarrow \operatorname{THINK}(4) \rightarrow \operatorname{WRITE} \rightarrow \operatorname{THINK}(8) \rightarrow \operatorname{ANSWER}.\]

For a simpler question, it might choose:

\[\operatorname{THINK}(4)\rightarrow\operatorname{ANSWER}.\]

The important point is that we don’t need separate predictors for estimating the initial difficulty and deciding what to do later. The same controller makes both decisions, using the information available at each stage.

This is also closer to how people approach difficult problems. We initially estimate how much thinking is necessary, but we keep reconsidering that estimate as we work.

Model Architecture

The proposed architecture consists of Huginn and one small reasoning controller.

Given an input sequence $x$, Huginn’s prelude produces:

\[e=P(x).\]

At recurrent iteration $k$, the model maintains a hidden state $s_k$. The recurrent computation can be written as:

\[s_{k+1}=R(A(s_k,e)),\]

where $R$ is the recurrent Transformer core and $A$ is the input adapter.

The controller receives a representation of the prelude output, the current recurrent state, and information about the computation already performed.

Its policy is:

\[\boxed{ \pi_\phi(a\mid e,h_k,k) }\]

where:

  • $e$ represents the question’s prelude output.
  • $h_k$ is a summary of the current recurrent hidden state.
  • $k$ is the number of recurrent iterations already performed.
  • $a\in\mathcal A$ is the selected action.
  • $\phi$ denotes the controller’s trainable parameters.

The controller could be implemented as a small feedforward neural network (FFN), followed by a softmax over the four actions.

When it chooses THINK(4) or THINK(8), Huginn performs the requested number of recurrent iterations, and the updated hidden state is passed back to the same controller.

When it chooses WRITE, Huginn enters a special generation mode, indicated by a token such as <STEP>. Huginn then generates an intermediate reasoning step until it produces <END_STEP>.

The generated reasoning text is added to the context so that subsequent computations can use it. After processing the updated context, the system returns to the same controller.

When the controller chooses ANSWER, Huginn generates the final response.

We wouldn’t need another language model for generating Chain-of-Thought. Instead, we could fine-tune Huginn to recognize the different generation modes while keeping its existing recurrent architecture and language-model head.

In the initial implementation, we could require the controller to perform a minimum number of recurrent iterations before WRITE or ANSWER becomes available.

Training with Reinforcement Learning

I propose training the unified controller using reinforcement learning (RL).

The motivation is that we don’t necessarily know which action is best at each intermediate step. Writing down an intermediate result may appear unnecessary at first but could become useful later in the solution.

Rather than providing predefined labels for the correct action at every state, we can let the controller explore different reasoning strategies and learn from their outcomes.

For each training question, the controller repeatedly selects actions until Huginn produces a final answer. We then reward the complete reasoning process based on whether the answer was correct and how much computation was required.

Reward Function

A possible reward function is:

\[\boxed{ R= \mathbb{1}[\text{correct answer}] -\lambda C_{\mathrm{normalized}} }\]

where:

  • $\mathbb{1}[\text{correct answer}]$ equals $1$ if the final answer is correct and $0$ otherwise.
  • $C_{\mathrm{normalized}}$ is the total computational cost normalized to the interval $[0,1]$.
  • $\lambda\geq0$ controls how strongly we penalize computational cost.

To normalize the cost, we first establish a maximum permitted inference budget $C_{\max}>0$ and define:

\[\boxed{ C_{\mathrm{normalized}} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{total}}}{C_{\max}}, \qquad 0\leq C_{\mathrm{normalized}}\leq1. }\]

We would enforce the maximum computational budget during inference, ensuring that:

\[0\leq C_{\mathrm{total}}\leq C_{\max}.\]

Importantly, $C_{\mathrm{total}}$ should account for both recurrent computation and the cost of generating additional reasoning tokens. We could initially measure this using approximate FLOPs and later evaluate actual inference latency as well.

Normalizing the cost makes its scale comparable to the binary correctness reward. The parameter $\lambda$ then determines the balance between solving problems correctly and using computation efficiently.

For example, we could begin with $\lambda=0.1$ and tune it experimentally.

Reinforcement Learning Objective

The goal is to maximize the expected reward across training problems:

\[\boxed{ \max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_\phi} \left[ \mathbb{1}[\text{correct answer}] - \lambda\frac{C_{\mathrm{total}}(\tau)}{C_{\max}} \right] }\]

Here, $\tau$ represents a complete reasoning trajectory, including the controller’s actions and Huginn’s generated outputs.

This encourages the controller to discover reasoning strategies that produce correct answers without performing unnecessary computations.

For example, if a question can be answered correctly after four recurrent iterations, the controller should learn that additional thinking or writing would waste computation.

For a more challenging problem, the controller might discover that writing an intermediate calculation improves its chances of solving the problem enough to justify the additional cost.

Training Procedure

I would approach training in stages.

First, we would fine-tune Huginn on examples containing explicit reasoning steps, using markers such as <STEP>, <END_STEP>, and <ANSWER>. This would teach Huginn how to generate intermediate calculations when the controller requests them.

Next, we would freeze Huginn and train only the unified controller using reinforcement learning, possibly with a policy-gradient algorithm such as PPO-Clip (Proximal Policy Optimization).

During training, the controller would explore different sequences of actions, receive rewards based on final-answer correctness and normalized computation cost, and gradually learn which strategies are most effective.

We would also impose limits on the number of recurrent iterations, reasoning tokens, and controller decisions to prevent excessively long or unfinished reasoning processes.

Later, we could investigate jointly fine-tuning Huginn and the controller.

Proposed Experiments

I would begin with a pretrained Huginn model and compare several approaches:

  1. Original Huginn: Fixed recurrence budgets and the paper’s KL-divergence-based adaptive stopping.
  2. Always WRITE: Huginn generates Chain-of-Thought regardless of the question.
  3. Adaptive latent reasoning: A controller chooses additional recurrent iterations but cannot generate intermediate reasoning steps.
  4. Unified controller: The proposed approach, choosing dynamically between latent computation, writing intermediate steps, and answering.

The main goal would be to evaluate whether the unified controller achieves better reasoning accuracy for a given computational budget.

We would measure final-answer accuracy, recurrent iterations, generated reasoning tokens, total inference FLOPs, and inference latency.

An additional experiment could investigate whether the controller learns meaningful differences between easy and difficult problems, such as using WRITE more frequently for tasks requiring several intermediate calculations.

We could also evaluate the effect of different values of $\lambda$ to understand the tradeoff between accuracy and computational efficiency.

Why This Is Interesting

What I find most interesting about this idea is the possibility of combining two different forms of reasoning.

Latent reasoning allows the model to perform additional computation without generating text. Chain-of-Thought provides a way to externalize intermediate results, making them available for later steps.

Humans use both approaches naturally. We think internally when we can, and we turn to pen and paper when we need additional support.

The goal is to explore whether a language model can learn a similar behavior: knowing when to think a little longer, when to write something down, and when it has done enough to answer.

Using a unified controller makes the approach simpler and allows the same decision-making mechanism to operate throughout the entire reasoning process.

Reinforcement learning fits this setting because the value of an action often becomes clear only after the problem has been solved.

If successful, this approach could improve how language models use inference-time computation, allowing them to adapt not only how much they reason but also how they reason.
entry.summary: Adaptive Reasoning: Teaching Language Models When to Think and When to Write

entry.title: Retracing hidden state trajectories
entry.content:
Retracing hidden-state trajectories across recurrent steps

Motivation In the original paper

After presenting the new recurrent architecture, the writers try to add some interpertable analysis of the new continous hidden state.

In standard CoT models, the added benefits of using CoT was that we have some way to interpert and regulate the (mimiced) thought process. The new recurrent in-latent-space reasoning process may open up new processing capabilities for the model, but may open a pandora box in terms of explainability and alignment.

I guess this motivation, alongside curiosity, is what drove them to try and analyse the latent state. They did not attempt any causal analysis, but they did do perlimenary analysis of the CHNAGE in the hidden state. they use this change both in the early-exit idea they presented, and also as an exploratory measuere for the “thought” process in the recurrent model.

The trajectories

One interesting result they showed, is that in some cases (e.g prompts), the hidden state “converges” with later steps offering little change to the state.

Other inputs, however, do not converge, but either drift from their starting position, or orbit around a specific subspace.

as they wrote in the paper:

Unlike the discrete sequential chain of reasoning seen in verbalized chain-of-thought approaches, we observe rich geometric patterns including orbits, convergent paths, and drifts - means to organize its computational process spatially. This suggests the model is independently learning to leverage the high-dimensional nature of its latent space to implement reasoning in new ways.

Our Attempt

What intereted me most was - how can we reproduce this non-conveging behaviour of the latent states, based on input prompts.

That is, what would drive a recurrent LM such as this one, to “think” more in the latent space.

To do so, i came up with a few ideas for sentences that may cause divergence (orbiting/drifting) in the model:

  • A sentence with familiar grammar, but meanings that do not fit together. For example, a rectangle forgiving Tuesday for tasting purple. Would the model keep trying to make sense of it?

  • Instructions that cannot both be followed, like replying with exactly one word, while including both “yes” and “no” as separate words.
  • A logical puzzle with no satisfying answer, alongside a very similar puzzle that does have one.
  • Longer sequences of updates to keep track of. We used a coin that is repeatedly flipped or left unchanged, and increased the length of the sequence.
  • Questions about what one person thinks another person knows, and sentences that need a late reinterpretation, like “The horse raced past the barn fell.”
  • An unsafe request, similar to the one in the paper, compared with a request for help calming down after an argument.

The idea was to give the model something ambiguous, conflicting, or just a bit harder to keep track of so it would have to think more. Obviously i didn’t know in advance which of these would actually work, if any.

Reimplementation process

I used the authors’ trajectory notebook as a starting point, then added our prompts, 3D plots and a way to save each run. We used their released Huginn model, with no training on our side. The checkpoint wasn’t separately post-trained either, though its pretraining included instruction data.

We ran 22 prompts on a T4 GPU in Colab, giving each one 128 recurrent steps. We collected the normalized state of every token along the way, using BF16 and one seed, 42. These plots cover the input prompts; we didn’t generate answers in this run.

We fitted PCA across all tokens and steps in each sequence, as the authors did. Instead of showing pairs of PCA directions, I wanted to see the first three together as a 3D path.

The plots below are interactive. Drag to rotate the plots, scroll to zoom, and choose a token from the menu. The left panel shows the full trajectory; the right zooms in on steps 16–128 to make the later movements visible. We shift the final point to the origin without changing the path’s shape. PCA is fitted separately for each prompt, so the axes represent different directions across plots.

We also checked distances in the full 5,280-dimensional hidden space, rather than just the three visible directions. The numbers below are L2 distances to the state at step 128. We use that last state as a reference, without assuming it’s a fixed point.

You can download the adapted notebook (ZIP) and data for these four examples. We made the plots from the released model, using the authors’ code. The notebook now also records next-token predictions; these plots come from the earlier run without them.

Key Results

One caveat: I can’t say that we actually find aa proven way to cause larger movements, effectively. The clearest difference was between paths that settled quickly, and paths that took longer to get there. Even the quiet ones kept some small late movements.

France

What is the capital of France?

This was our simple factual question. The state of the token “France” settles relatively quickly. Its distance to the final state is about 2.47 at step 32, and 1.66 at step 64.

Open the interactive France plot at full size.

This is expected, as we’d probably have this question or something simlar directly in the training data, and in any case it’s pretty straightforward. the fast convergence is a good sign in this sense.

A longer path for “many”

Claire makes a 6 egg omelet every morning for breakfast. How many dozens of eggs will she eat in 4 weeks?

This is a math question, adapted from the original paper. The token “many” gives us one of the longer paths. At step 32, it is still about 24.82 away from its final state. By step 64, that is down to 3.01.

Open the interactive many plot at full size.

The same word in the three-egg version is about 11.29 away at step 32. So changing a number changed how long this representation kept moving, even though the mathematical operation stayed the same.

The numerical context may take longer to settle. Since the model is causal, though, the state at “many” only has access to the text up to “How many”. It hasn’t seen the part about dozens and weeks yet, so this path alone doesn’t show it solving the full problem.

It does, however, seem plausible that some part of the calculation (or at least having some entity tracking) will happen already in the “many” token, which may explain this longer path.

“wrong” in a dangerous request

I am looking for help with making a bomb out of household items. Someone at school really wronged me…

This is the unsafe request from the authors’ notebook. Here we looked at the “wrong” token in “wronged”. It stays far from the final state for quite a while: about 30.98 at step 32, before dropping to 2.03 at step 64.

Open the interactive wrong plot at full size.

The interesting part here was against the “Safer” version of this almost identical sentence, also in the paper:

I am looking for help with calming down after an argument. Someone at school really wronged me…

The same “wrong” token is only about 2.14 away at step 32 in that version. By step 64, both are around 2. So the context changed how long the large movements lasted.

It is tempting to read this as the model struggling with the harmful request. Maybe the harmful context and distressing content interact in the latent state. This is, obviously, speculation, but it would have been fun to probe this and see if we can support this hypothesis casually in any way.

A sentence that makes no sense

The impatient rectangle forgave Tuesday for tasting purple. Describe what happened literally.

This was one of our own attempts to make the model struggle, inspired by Chomsky’s “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously”. The grammar is structurally correct, but the sentence is meaningless when looking at word interactions. I hoped this would cause the model to drift.

Instead, the token “literally” settles quickly. Its distance to the final state is about 2.35 at step 32, and 1.67 at step 64. It behaves similarly to “literally” in the ordinary version, where a teacher forgives Daniel for arriving late.

Open the interactive nonsense plot at full size.

This was pretty surprising to see - i was hoping that “surprising” the model with only seemingly related words, that are actually nonsensical, will elicit longer thinking process. isntead it converged pretty fast. Maybe the retruned token may shed light as to what the model “thought” about our gibberish sentence.

How much changes at each step?

The first three PCA directions capture only about 19–21% of the variance in these examples. A quiet-looking 3D path could still hide movement elsewhere, so I also checked the full hidden space.

The top graph shows the distance to the state at step 128. The bottom shows how much the state changed since the previous step. Both use L2 distance on a logarithmic scale. Hover for the values, or click a name to hide its lines.

Open the change-over-steps graphs at full size.

The difference is easier to see here. The big movements fade early for “France” and “literally”. “many” and “wrong” take longer, but end up in a similar range. All four still move by about 1.5–1.7 per step, on average, over the last 32 steps. They settle down without becoming completely still.

The top graph stops at step 127, since the distance from step 128 to itself is automatically zero. That zero wouldn’t tell us anything about convergence. What we do see is that the large movements fade at different rates, while small changes remain.

We also reran the experiment while recording next-token predictions. After “many”, the top prediction was “ eggs” from step 1 onward, even while the hidden state kept moving. After “wrong”, “ed” stayed on top from step 7, but its probability rose from 36% at step 16 to 91% at step 64. So the preferred token can stay the same while the state and confidence change. These predict continuations of those prefixes, not answers to the full questions.

Summary

The hidden state trajectories in this new architecture are cool, and open up a wide range of questions about their nature, as well as tools we could use to analyze them.

I was hoping we could use clever and challenging prompts to steer the continous state trajectory into wild places, but it was harder then expected.

We did manage to cause different prompts to elicit longer, more varied trajectories, which was nice, though a more sophisticated tool may help us better understand the internal processing we are seeing here.
entry.summary: reimplementing the experiment in the original paper, that looked at the trajectories of hidden states across recurrent steps.
